clock.basis: The NWS Birmingham survey prints its start and end as 443 pm and 614 pm with no time zone beside them. The same page gives the parent storm's times in CDT, and the retained NCEI county records begin and end at the same two instants in CST, so this chronology reads the survey labels as CDT, five hours behind UTC. The December 2011 assessment prints its Table 1 interval under a column headed Time (CST), and those labels are converted as printed, six hours behind UTC. Minute labels retain source precision, not measured clock accuracy. Between entries, the player holds the last documentary record. It does not interpolate storm positions, images or impacts.

sources.title: NWS Birmingham survey of the Tuscaloosa and Birmingham tornado (undated web page, text archived November 14, 2026)
NWS Service Assessment, The Historic Tornadoes of April 2011, December 2011

entries.title: Approximate start in the survey
entries.account: The survey gives an approximate start point of 33.0297/-87.9350 at 443 pm. The survey bases the start point on aerial survey. The tornado touched down in rural northern Greene County and moved northeast toward Tuscaloosa.
entries.limits: The survey calls this time approximate and gives no error bound. The NCEI Greene County record begins at 15:43 CST, the same instant, but both come from the same agency survey, so their agreement is not an independent check.
entries.locator: Summary box, Approximate Start Point/Time, and the survey narrative that follows it.

entries.source_time: 3:50 – 4:45 p.m., in a column headed Time (CST)
entries.title: Assessment Table 1 interval begins
entries.account: Table 1 of the December 2011 assessment lists the Tuscaloosa and Jefferson tornado from 3:50 to 4:45 p.m. under a column headed Time (CST). Read as CST, the interval begins at 4:50 p.m. CDT.
entries.limits: This interval disagrees with the survey and the report does not explain why. Read as printed, 3:50 to 4:45 p.m. CST is 4:50 to 5:45 p.m. CDT, which starts 7 minutes after the survey's approximate start and ends 29 minutes before its approximate end. If the column label were wrong and the times were CDT, the interval would end 2 minutes after the survey's start. This chronology shows both sources and does not choose between them.
entries.locator: Printed page 6, Table 1, row for Tuscaloosa, Jefferson AL.

entries.source_time: 3:50 – 4:45 p.m., in a column headed Time (CST)
entries.title: Assessment Table 1 interval ends
entries.account: The same Table 1 row ends at 4:45 p.m. in its CST column, which is 5:45 p.m. CDT. The survey places the tornado still on the ground at this minute.
entries.limits: This interval disagrees with the survey and the report does not explain why. Read as printed, 3:50 to 4:45 p.m. CST is 4:50 to 5:45 p.m. CDT, which starts 7 minutes after the survey's approximate start and ends 29 minutes before its approximate end. If the column label were wrong and the times were CDT, the interval would end 2 minutes after the survey's start. This chronology shows both sources and does not choose between them.
entries.locator: Printed page 6, Table 1, row for Tuscaloosa, Jefferson AL.

entries.title: Approximate end in the survey
entries.account: The survey gives an approximate end point of 33.6311/-86.7436 at 614 pm. The survey says a ground crew determined the end location. The tornado lifted just west of Alabama Highway 79, about 2 miles north of Tarrant.
entries.limits: The survey calls this time approximate and gives no error bound. The NCEI Jefferson County record ends at 17:14 CST, the same instant, from the same agency survey. The parent storm later produced the separate Ohatchee tornado, which is not part of this track.
entries.locator: Summary box, Approximate End Point/Time, and the final paragraph of the survey narrative.
